This raises an important question: how much Bitcoin should you include in your portfolio? Their 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions predict a 10% annual return for Bitcoin over the next 10 to 15 years. This outpaces their projections for U.S. large-cap stocks at 7.5% and U.S. REITs at 8.2%. However, Bitcoin carries high risk, with estimated annual volatility of 55%. As of October 22, 2026, Bitcoin is trading around $82,000, roughly 22% lower than a year ago. Given these figures, does a potential 10% return justify allocating 10% of your portfolio to Bitcoin? Investors who typically use a 60/40 mix of stocks and bonds may question whether their portfolio lacks diversity. Some may take bold steps; for instance, a recent Reddit post on r/wallstreetbets shared a user’s experience of investing almost all their liquid assets in Bitcoin and Strategy (NASDAQ: MSTR), the largest corporate Bitcoin holder, which drew significant attention. Remember, the 10% return averages over many years. It doesn’t indicate where Bitcoin’s price will be in the coming year, and this forecast could include years of substantial losses. Bitcoin’s significant volatility plays a more critical role in shaping your investment outcome than its potential 10% return. How much Bitcoin you hold in your portfolio determines how much a significant downturn can affect your overall investment. A 50% drop in Bitcoin’s price will impact your portfolio based on your Bitcoin allocation. Here’s how Bitcoin allocations can affect your portfolio during a drop: Beyond the risk of drastic price drops, Bitcoin can also swing wildly in shorter time frames. For instance, while Bitcoin surged about 31% over the past 90 days, it remains 22% lower than it was a year ago. Excluding Bitcoin altogether eliminates the 55% volatility, but it also forgoes the potential for higher returns. This strategy may suit individuals nearing retirement or those who would panic and sell after a significant drop. A 1% or 5% allocation with regular rebalancing lets you benefit from Bitcoin’s upside while reducing the potential damage of a crash. For example, if your 5% Bitcoin investment doubles while your other investments stay the same, your Bitcoin slice would grow to about 9.5% of your portfolio. Rebalancing can help lock in gains by selling some Bitcoin to return to your original 5% allocation. This rebalancing strategy also works well after a price drop, as it lets you maintain your desired allocation without letting your Bitcoin exposure dwindle to almost nothing. Keep in mind the tax implications: selling Bitcoin in a taxable account may trigger capital gains tax, while a spot Bitcoin ETF in an IRA can be adjusted without immediate tax consequences. By contrast, a 10% Bitcoin allocation or more—especially through a leveraged investment like Strategy—might not be advisable for most households. With a 10% Bitcoin allocation, a 50% drop reduces the entire portfolio’s value by 5%. Furthermore, swapping Bitcoin for a leverage-dependent asset amplifies risk, which is something only investors with a long time horizon, solid cash reserves, and the ability to endure downturns should consider. For most investors interested in Bitcoin, aiming for a smaller allocation—around 1% or 5%—is generally more sensible. This conservatively sized investment accounts for the high volatility while aligning with the potential for favorable returns. This approach suits individuals who have already secured their emergency fund and retirement savings and can hold through significant fluctuations without selling their Bitcoin. Successful investing depends on sizing your position based on volatility rather than chasing headlines about potential returns. Many investors jump in after big gains and sell into losses, ultimately doing worse than steady investors. It helps to set a rebalancing rule, such as reviewing your allocation once a year. If J.P. title: Finding opportunities in Asia equities amid the selloff - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. After a powerful run in AI and technology equities, October has delivered a sharp reminder that winning investments rarely move in a straight line. Semiconductors – which have been leading for most of the AI rally – saw a sharp selloff as the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index posted one of its longest losing streaks since 2008. It fell eight consecutive sessions through mid-October to and currently trades at 20% off year-to-date peaks. Closely-related tech-heavy markets in Asia such as Taiwan and Korea are also down by around 10% and 30% from peak levels respectively. The catalysts are familiar. There seems to be a constant flow doubt over the AI story. From uncertainties over Anthropic’s near-term revenue trajectory reigniting debates over the economics of the AI buildout, neocloud credit availability questioning 2028 capex assumptions, to headlines around data-center project delays and intensifying voter and political opposition ahead of the midterm elections – many factors have added to market volatility. Some questions are dominating client conversations: Is the AI capex cycle sustainable, or are we approaching a top? Are valuations in AI winners stretched to the point where the risk-reward is no longer attractive? How should investors think about near-term technical pressures such as narrow market leadership, concentration within indices and financing concerns as rates rise? Some Asian markets have been core to the AI buildout and have delivered market-leading returns – but are most of the returns behind us? As we stand at the start of the fourth quarter, this has broadly been a positive year of equity returns in aggregate for Asia despite the recent selloff. However, there has also been large divergence in equity returns, with Korea and Taiwan delivering around 60% returns YTD (USD terms) while China's Offshore and India's equity markets have declined by around 15%. Similar to the US, parts of Asia have been undergoing an earnings super-cycle due to the ongoing AI infrastructure buildout, and this is one key reason driving a divergence in earnings revisions so far this year. Investors have rewarded markets with earnings upside, while rightfully penalizing those with weaker earnings outlooks. In this week’s Asia Strategy Focus, we dive deeper into the earnings progress across the Asian equities landscape in the first nine months of 2026, and detail our thoughts and investment outlook going forward. Starting with Korea, due to the ongoing memory shortage as AI demand outstrips supply, earnings expectations for 2026/2027 have seen an incredible 183%/243% positive revision since the beginning of the year. This has been the driving force for the impressive market returns year-to-date. Understandably, investors are questioning the sustainability of these earnings, and the valuation multiple for Korea has declined by over 50% to just a 4x forward P/E. We came into the year positive on Korean equities, and this remains one of our preferred regions. We continue to be of the view that memory supply and demand will likely stay tight at least into 2028 and potentially beyond. The risk/reward skews positively at this juncture in the markets after the significant near-term pullback. Similarly, Taiwan has been the key manufacturer of leading-edge logic chips that are used for training and inferencing in the rapid adoption of AI across the world. With semiconductors and tech hardware representing 86% of the MSCI Taiwan Index, it provides direct exposure and is a clear beneficiary across the entire AI supply chain. This has driven positive earnings revisions of 38%/53% for 2026/2027 and has been the key driver of Taiwan's above-market returns in 2026. With our current expectations for 2026/2027 earnings to grow by 69%/33%, we view Taiwan's valuation at 18x forward P/E as attractive and continue to recommend the region. Taiwan, alongside Korea, remains some of the cleanest expressions of the global AI hardware theme and sits at the heart of our preferred Asia equity positioning. There have also been notable detractors in Asia equity markets – both Offshore China and Onshore China's equity performance so far this year has been underwhelming. With the domestic economy showing continued signs of slowing down, local governments prioritizing fiscal consolidation, a stronger currency, and heavy AI capital expenditure weighing on reported earnings, this has translated into 2026/2027 consensus expectations declining by 6%/5% through September this year. We have been tactical with Offshore China equities this year and lowered our recommendation at the end of August to neutral given these growing headwinds. We currently expect earnings growth in 2026/2027 of 9%/12%, and with a valuation at 10x forward P/E, we do not find Offshore China compelling and retain our neutral view. We continue to monitor policy support, AI localization progress – where local chips are expected to meet 80% of China's AI infrastructure demand by 2028 – and the pace of internet-platform monetization as potential catalysts for a more constructive stance. Many of the macro headwinds this year, including higher oil prices, a stronger US dollar, and rising global interest rates, have been challenges for the Indian equity market. With the added concern of AI disruption risk for labor outsourcing businesses such as call centers and IT consulting, it is unsurprising that the Indian equity market has underperformed. This is apparent in earnings, which have seen negative revisions of -3.5% in 2027. We have also witnessed a de-rating in the premium valuation that Indian equities have historically commanded relative to Asian equities, as earnings growth is currently less impressive compared to other Asian regions. With an expected earnings growth in 2027/2028 of just 7%/11% and a valuation at 18.4x forward P/E, we do not find the risk/reward attractive and keep our neutral rating. Longer-term structural themes – including physical AI, electronics manufacturing, defense, and a power grid buildout – remain compelling, but the near-term earnings profile does not yet justify a more constructive stance. Similar to developed markets such as the US and Europe, Japan has seen exceptionally strong earnings revisions this year, with 2026/2027 estimates now 16%/14% higher than at the beginning of 2026, and this has driven the TOPIX higher by 17% year-to-date. While technology has benefited from the AI infrastructure buildout, there has also been broad strength across other sectors such as industrials and financials, where rate hikes from the Bank of Japan rate have been particularly impactful. While we hold a positive view on the earnings growth outlook for Japan at 25%/8% in 2026/2027, we find valuations at a forward P/E of 16x mildly high relative to history. We retain a neutral view on Japan and await a better entry point before turning more decidedly positive. In the next couple of weeks, markets are receiving earnings results from the large US hyperscalers and semiconductor supply chain companies, and the midterm elections will be concluded, which could remove some of the uncertainties and overhangs in the market at the moment. Looking further ahead, as we put forth in a previous report on Emerging Markets, EM is no longer just a tactical trade on low valuations – it is increasingly a strategic allocation to the industries the world now needs most: semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, critical commodities, and AI infrastructure. Asia sits at the core of that case. Taiwan and Korea offer direct beta to global AI compute through the hardware and memory supply chains, while China provides selective exposure to AI localization and platforms. For investors seeking to express the theme more broadly, thematic strategies spanning the AI value chain and EM equity managers can complement single-country exposure. Our message to investors is to stay allocated to AI and tech as the capex cycle, earnings trajectory, and supply-demand backdrop remain intact. We view the current volatility as an opportunity to add high-conviction exposure on weakness rather than a reason to retreat. However, right-sizing those allocations is key. The concentration risk is real: Korea and Taiwan already represent more than half of the MSCI EM (Emerging Markets) Index, and significant overweights could leave portfolios heavily dependent on a single theme. Pair conviction AI exposure with uncorrelated sources of return, and maintain diversification across regions and asset classes. The recent market volatility is uncomfortable, but it is the price of admission to one of the most important investment themes of this decade. Our conviction remains unchanged – and the dispersion within Asia offers a rich opportunity set. title: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley are dominating the AI stock boom. Here's their edge - CNBC
content:
Fueled by the global boom in artificial intelligence stocks, relaxed capital rules and greater lending to hedge funds, big Wall Street banks have already had a banner year for equities trading — even with one quarter left to go. The five biggest investment banks have generated about $67 billion in equities revenue through Sept. 30, according to company filings. That is $7 billion more than what the group made during all of 2025, which itself was a record haul. But it’s Wall Street’s Big Three that have captured the largest slice of what is shaping up to be the industry’s most lucrative arena: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase and Morgan Stanley have made a combined $52 billion in stock trading revenue so far this year, nearly 80% of the total. “When it comes to the AI mega trade, the Big Three consider each other their main competitors, and that’s pretty much it,” Mike Mayo, Wells Fargo banking analyst, told CNBC. “They’ve been best positioned to take advantage of this market.” Wall Street banks are experiencing an epic run of blockbuster profits as the total value of the stock market balloons and trading activity from institutional and retail investors rises across stocks, exchange-traded funds and derivatives. Helping drive this activity are the loans that the banks, through their prime brokerages, are extending to hedge funds so that they can amplify their bets. Prime brokerage — the business of providing hedge funds with margin loans, securities lending and other trading services — has become a key battleground and source of growth. The Big Three’s prime brokers are central to the larger equities story because they serve the largest funds across markets and products. Demand for leverage to make bets on AI hardware, hyperscalers and chip suppliers has reached new heights, bank executives said last week. At Goldman Sachs, equities financing activities jumped 96% in the third quarter to a record $3.37 billion. JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley don’t break out that figure, but said they saw a similar dynamic. “I like your ‘insatiable demand for capital’ point. That feels about right,” JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said on the bank’s third-quarter conference call, responding to analyst questions about financing demands. “In this moment where AI is such an overwhelming theme ... there is capital being tapped through all kinds of different mechanisms,” Barnum said. That demand has helped transform equity desks at the Big Three from cyclical, transactional businesses into more durable, high-margin lending engines, Wall Street executives say. The performance gap between Wall Street’s giants and rivals including Bank of America and Citigroup highlights a widening divide in capital markets. “For clients, the value isn’t just a price on one trade, it’s coverage and continuity,” Rachid Alaoui, JPMorgan global head of equities, told CNBC in an interview. “You want a dealer that can give you the full suite across products, and you want that service to travel with you across regions. That matters in stressed markets and periods of volatility.” Executing multibillion-dollar bets, like leveraged swaps on volatile AI stocks or sector ETFs, can require an enormous balance sheet. The biggest banks can absorb potential $100 million losses without threatening their quarters, according to trading executives. Smaller or more niche banks can’t underwrite single-trade risks of that magnitude, forcing them to decline the business or cede share. U.S. prime brokers have also benefited from the retreat of European banks including Credit Suisse from the equities business, said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Herman Chan. “Prime is one of the ultimate scale businesses,” Chan said. “If you have a strong equities franchise, the hedge funds will want to transact with you because you have a bigger pool of trading opportunities with counterparties.” While U.S. markets were swept up in software and cloud computing giants this year, trading executives say the fastest-growing frontier for equities was in Asia. Institutional investors poured into South Korea and Taiwan, targeting the “picks and shovels” of the AI supply chain: the memory chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers supporting data center construction, Alaoui said. For the Big Three, with their footprints across Tokyo; Hong Kong; Seoul, South Korea; and Mumbai, India; the Asia trade was a goldmine. However, trading executives point out that transaction taxes and stamp duties are included in top-line revenue, artificially inflating Asia prime totals. There is also no agreed-upon definition of what equities trading revenue should include, so some banks include business lines like clearing services that others exclude from their stock trading totals, making apples-to-apples comparisons difficult. But that doesn’t change the overall momentum of the business, boosted by a stock rally that began in October 2022, weeks before OpenAI released ChatGPT. “We’re still in a stock-based world,” Morgan Stanley CEO Ted Pick said on the firm’s earnings call. “Equities are still, all things being equal, the attractive asset class.” While the CEOs of Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley have said the AI build-out is still in its early years, if AI turns out to be not as transformative as hoped, a downturn could impact those banks more than others, analysts said. The boom has also drawn some concern over the possible risks posed by hedge funds. The International Monetary Fund warned this month that growing leverage, crowded positions and correlated selling from hedge funds could create potential stability risks. The IMF estimated that global hedge fund assets had reached $13 trillion. In August, JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said industrywide leverage was “the highest it’s ever been,” though he stopped short of calling the risk big enough to pose a threat to the financial markets. Wall Street executives and analysts pointed out that the industry wasn’t fazed by the meltdown of several hedge funds this summer. While the hedge fund run by former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner, Situational Awareness, garnered the most headlines, several smaller firms also experienced a forced unwinding. Prime brokers have learned to leap on margin calls and quickly take down risk when markets move against clients, JPMorgan’s Alaoui said. “In the summer, some investors had positions they were forced to unwind,” he told CNBC. “They deleveraged, risk came down, and the market moved on.” Another factor driving the equities boom: Trump administration regulators have eased some leverage rules for the largest U.S. banks, giving them more room to expand balance sheet-heavy businesses including prime brokerage. The revised rules were finalized in 2025, and banks were allowed to adopt them as early as January. By easing the stringent balance sheet caps that previously treated Treasurys and prime brokerage loans, which are collateralized, the same as riskier assets, regulators gave dealers greater flexibility to deploy balance sheet capital. “Capital did go down, so you have to say the system is somewhat more levered because of the relaxation in regulations,” said Darrell Duffie, a finance professor at Stanford University and a leading expert on financial stability. “It’s not a good idea, but it hasn’t gotten dramatically out of whack.” The larger size of the market and higher volatility can create more trading, derivatives activity and leverage, he said, but that’s not inherently alarming. Wall Street executives also downplayed concerns over leverage, pointing out that they use collateral and frequent stress testing to get ahead of problems. “Hedge fund leverage as a contributor of risk to the system is very much in the category of known unknowns,” JPMorgan’s Barnum said last week. “It doesn’t mean it’s riskless, but we kind of know what it is.” — CNBC’s Leslie Picker and Ritika Shah contributed to this report. According to Kinexys, it has processed over $4 trillion in transactions since its inception, averaging about $7 billion each day. However, much of this transaction volume occurs on JPMorgan’s private Kinexys network, which operates separately from its public blockchain activities. The bank hasn’t disclosed how much of its total activity occurs on Ethereum or Base. JPM Coin is essentially a deposit token, where each coin represents a U.S. dollar deposited in a client’s account at JPMorgan. Retail investors are unable to buy or hold it, and all holders must have the bank’s approval. The bank chose the Ethereum network for its greater liquidity than other options and its existing institutional user base. The deposit-token structure also benefits JPMorgan; when clients hold JPM Coin, the dollars remain on the bank’s balance sheet as deposits. This allows the bank to continue lending those funds and earning interest, even as the cash moves to public blockchains. JPM Coin creates a direct link to ETH because every transaction on the Ethereum mainnet incurs a gas fee, which users pay in ETH. Increased institutional activity on Ethereum could modestly increase demand for ETH to cover these fees. However, each JPM Coin corresponds to one dollar. Clients only need a minimal amount of ETH for transaction fees, and JPMorgan does not require clients to hold ETH as an investment. The bank has not set a volume target for its Ethereum transactions, nor has it disclosed how many clients are utilizing the token on the mainnet. Base serves as a useful reference point. JPM Coin has been active there since November 2025, and Base fees are also paid in ETH. However, JPMorgan has not provided any usage statistics for Base, leaving it unclear how much demand there is for ETH in that context. The competitive landscape further constrains JPM Coin’s potential. Existing non-bank stablecoins dominate the dollar token market on Ethereum, and JPMorgan and other major banks reportedly plan a shared tokenized deposit network that could challenge both stablecoins and crypto firms. Such a network could draw bank activity toward systems they directly control. Market trends also do not indicate a positive outlook. ETH fell by 10.4% in October leading up to October 19. On October 18, it closed 5.9% below its 20-day average and 5.6% below its 50-day average, suggesting a downward trend. Additionally, spot Ether ETFs experienced net outflows of $103 million on October 19, the day JPM Coin launched on Ethereum. This outflow indicates that investors pulled out more money than they added. Notably, BlackRock’s iShares Ethereum Trust (NASDAQ:ETHA) accounted for $95 million of that total. In our view, JPM Coin is unlikely to significantly increase ETH’s price in the near future. JPMorgan made its JPM Coin deposit token available on Ethereum on Oct. 19, giving its institutional clients another public-blockchain route to send and receive dollar deposits. The launch adds Ethereum's main network alongside the token's existing availability on Base. JPMorgan says the expansion puts native cash on the network where institutions already transact with tokenized assets, collateral and counterparties. That includes its own tokenized money-market funds, bringing the bank's payment and investment offerings onto the same public blockchain. JPM Coin, which uses the ticker JPMD, digitally represents a bank deposit. The bank's Ethereum announcement says it supports peer-to-peer transfers between institutional clients in the Ethereum Virtual Machine ecosystem, including Base and Ethereum. Participation remains tied to the bank's institutional client base. A public network does not make the service available to every Ethereum wallet holder, and the announcement includes no retail rollout. The new route broadens where those clients can transact. In November 2025, JPM Coin became available to institutional clients on Base on November 12, after the proof of concept had begun in June 2025. Base is an Ethereum Layer 2 network. The October launch adds the Layer 1 network itself, extending the deposit token's reach within the Ethereum ecosystem. The deposit token joins investment products already on Ethereum. JPMorgan Asset Management launched My OnChain Net Yield Fund, or MONY, on Ethereum on Dec. 15, 2025. The private-placement money market fund is available to qualified investors through Morgan Money, the firm's investment platform.
